title: IT Band Syndrome Secondary to Osteogenic Cysts of the Proximal Tibia: A Rare Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Chronic localized pain over the proximal tibia is most often attributed to tendinopathy, degenerative disease, stress fracture, or benign bone lesions. Osteogenic cysts of the proximal tibia are rare and are usually considered as primary lesions in the differential diagnosis of a cortical lucency. It is far less recognized that such a cyst can act as a secondary trigger for chronic friction against the overlying iliotibial (IT) band, producing IT band syndrome as a consequence of the underlying bony pathology rather than as an independent process. We report a rare case in which IT band syndrome developed secondary to an osteogenic cyst of the proximal tibia. Case presentation A 45-year-old woman presented with several months of progressively worsening pain over the anterolateral aspect of the left proximal leg, aggravated by walking, prolonged standing, and stair climbing, without preceding trauma or constitutional symptoms. Examination revealed localized tenderness over the lateral proximal tibia, with pain on terminal knee movements. Plain radiographs showed a small, well-defined mixed lesion of the proximal tibia over lateral aspect, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a well-circumscribed cortical lesion with surrounding marrow edema and reactive soft-tissue change. Surgical exploration confirmed an intraosseous osteogenic cyst measuring 2.2 × 1.5 cm, with an adjacent, secondarily thickened fibrous band arising from chronic irritation of the IT band by the underlying cyst. fluoroscopy guided assessment of the lesion confirmed cystic material with a bony, cement-like consistency, in keeping with an osteogenic cyst. Complete excision of the cystic contents and the reactive fibrous band was performed. Histopathology confirmed bony material within the lesion, together with dense fibrocollagenous tissue and fibroblastic proliferation in the adjacent band, consistent with cyst-driven IT band syndrome. The patient had complete resolution of symptoms without recurrence at follow-up. Conclusions An osteogenic cyst of the proximal tibia can be an underrecognized secondary cause of IT band syndrome through chronic frictional irritation of the overlying band. Awareness of this association supports earlier imaging-directed diagnosis, appropriate intraoperative exploration, and complete excision of both the cyst and the reactive soft-tissue changes, which together provide excellent clinical outcomes.

title: Comparing Quantitative CT Patterns in Silicosis and Welder’s Pneumoconiosis: Significant Correlations with Lung Function and Identification of a Bimodal Histogram Pattern
abstract: Abstract Background: Given its progressive nature and compensation requirements, early diagnosis and objective monitoring of pneumoconiosis are essential. This study compared quantitative computed tomography (QCT) patterns in silicosis and welder’s pneumoconiosis (WP) and assessed their correlation with lung function. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 60 patients with pneumoconiosis, comprising 30 with silicosis and 30 with WP. Two radiologists, blinded to exposure data, performed QCT analysis. QCT parameters were compared between the study groups. Spearman correlation analyses were conducted between pulmonary function tests (PFTs) and QCT parameters, and between PFTs and the International Labour Organisation (ILO) classification categories. Results: In the silicosis group, a second peak, typically clustered within the range of -200 to +200 Hounsfield units (HU), was observed. This “Secondary peak” (bimodal histogram) was significantly associated with silica exposure, higher perfusion categories, and larger opacity sizes (p = 0.001, 0.007, and <0.001, respectively). Mean lung density showed a moderate negative correlation with both forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1, rho = −0.46) and forced vital capacity (FVC, rho = −0.53), whereas no significant association was found between ILO classification and PFTs. Conclusion: We defined the secondary peak in histogram analysis, linking it to increased opacity size, profusion, and silica exposure. QCT, which better reflects lung function than the ILO classification, may represent a promising option for monitoring pneumoconiosis.

title: An Extra-gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor Masquerading as an Adrenal Mass: A Case Report and Review of the Literature
abstract: Abstract Background: Extra-gastrointestinal stromal tumors (EGISTs) are rare mesenchymal neoplasms arising outside the gastrointestinal tract, most often in the omentum, mesentery, or retroperitoneum. Presentation as a suprarenal mass mimicking primary adrenal pathology is exceedingly uncommon, with only isolated cases reported in the literature. We describe the clinical course, diagnostic evaluation, surgical management, and pathological findings of a retroperitoneal EGIST that was preoperatively presumed an adrenocortical carcinoma. Case Presentation: A 74-year-old woman presented with left flank pain. Computed tomography (CT) imaging demonstrated a 5.8 x 6.1 x 4.9 cm heterogeneous left suprarenal mass with central necrosis, raising concern for adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC), pheochromocytoma, or metastatic disease. Comprehensive hormonal evaluation was negative. CT of the chest confirmed no metastatic disease. The patient underwent robot-assisted retroperitoneal laparoscopic left adrenalectomy with periaortic lymph node dissection. Final pathology revealed a low-grade GIST (spindle cell type, 7.5 cm, CD117+) arising from retroperitoneal soft tissue with the adrenal gland identified as a separate, uninvolved structure. Staging: pT3N0M0R1 (0/4 lymph nodes positive). The patient was discharged on postoperative day 2 without complications. Conclusion: GIST should be included in the differential of large retroperitoneal suprarenal masses. Immunohistochemistry — particularly CD117 (c-Kit) — is essential for definitive diagnosis. KIT/PDGFRA mutational analysis is mandatory to guide adjuvant tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy. Multidisciplinary oncologic review is warranted given the R1 resection and paucity of outcome data for retroperitoneal EGISTs.

title: Development and Internal Validation of Prediction Models for Early CT- Defined Moderate-to-Large Pleural Effusion After Liver Transplantation: a Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: Abstract Background Pleural effusion is common after liver transplantation (LT), but early moderate-to-large effusions remain difficult to predict. We developed and internally validated models for a study-specific computed tomography (CT)-defined severe postoperative pleural effusion (SPPE) endpoint. Methods We retrospectively studied LT recipients treated from June 2023 to January 2026. Patients with preoperative pleural effusion or unavailable postoperative chest imaging were excluded. SPPE was defined as a new effusion within 5 postoperative days with a maximum CT-estimated pleural-fluid depth ≥ 4 cm. The cohort was divided into a training set (n = 95) and a held-out validation set (n = 32). Four LASSO-selected predictors were used in five models. Conditional out-of-fold and 1000-replicate bootstrap validation kept predictors and hyperparameters fixed. Results Among 127 recipients, 78 (61.4%) met the SPPE definition. Retained predictors were previous abdominal surgery and immediate postoperative prognostic nutritional index (PNI), C-reactive protein, and aspartate aminotransferase measured within 1 hour after LT. Logistic regression achieved the highest held-out AUC (0.658; 95% confidence interval, 0.453–0.864). Bootstrap-corrected AUCs ranged from 0.710 to 0.761. Random forest had the highest corrected AUC (0.761) but the greatest optimism (0.079), whereas logistic regression had a corrected AUC of 0.734 and the lowest optimism (0.026). PNI was the only predictor with a nominally significant post-selection coefficient (odds ratio, 0.868; P = 0.010). Conclusions Discrimination was modest, and model ranking depended on the validation method. No algorithm was consistently superior. Prospective external validation is required before clinical use.

title: Toward Optimising Multiple Sclerosis MRI Protocols: A Comparative Study of Lesion Detection and Quantitative Image Quality Across MRI Sequences
abstract: Abstract Background Multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnosis relies on MRI lesion detection, yet conventional 2D FLAIR is limited by partial volume effects. This study combines per-lesion detection between 2D and 3D FLAIR, and evaluates quantitative image quality metrics across T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and 3D FLAIR at the patient level. Methods This retrospective, comparative imaging study included 23 patients diagnosed with MS according to the 2017 McDonald criteria, who underwent brain MRI on a 1.5 T scanner between November 2025 and June 2026. Each patient underwent both 2D and 3D FLAIR within the same examination, enabling head-to-head comparison of overall lesion count. Two board-certified radiologists independently counted lesions, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) were measured on T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and 3D FLAIR images. Analysis included paired-samples t-test, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, effect size (Cohen’s d) and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Results 3D FLAIR detected significantly more lesions than 2D FLAIR (1229 versus 897 overall, corresponding to a median of 56 versus 38 lesions per-patient; a 37% increase; p < 0.001), with excellent inter-rater agreement for both sequences (ICC = 0.988 and 0.993, respectively; both p < 0.001). T2-weighted imaging demonstrated the highest overall SNR (33.73 ± 12.39) and CNR (13.32 ± 7.79), followed by 3D FLAIR (SNR 19.89 ± 5.59; CNR 10.91 ± 5.62), and T1-weighted imaging (SNR 9.03 ± 4.15; CNR 6.57 ± 3.39) (all p < 0.021). Effect size analysis showed very large differences in SNR between 3D FLAIR and both T1- and T2-weighted (d = 1.48 and d = 1.54, respectively), and medium to medium-large in CNR (d = 0.66 and d = 0.52, respectively). Conclusion 3D FLAIR substantially improves overall lesion detection over conventional 2D FLAIR, while T2-weighted imaging offers superior contrast for lesion delineation. These complementary strengths support incorporating 3D FLAIR and T2-weighted imaging within a hybrid MS imaging protocol where feasible to improve lesion burden assessment.

title: Multi-Feature 3D Deep Learning for Predicting Antidepressant Treatment Response from Structural MRI
abstract: Abstract Objective Accurate prediction of treatment response in Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) remains a significant challenge due to individual neuroanatomical heterogeneity and the inherent scarcity of labeled clinical data. To address these limitations, we propose MAN-MDDNet, a 3D deep learning framework designed for early and precise prognosis by leveraging multi-feature structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI). Methods MAN-MDDNet leverages 3D anatomical representations learned from large-scale medical datasets to overcome the “small-sample” bottleneck typical in neuroimaging, ensuring robust feature convergence and stability. The model is inherently brain-structure-driven and uniquely fuses four complementary features—gray matter volume/density and white matter volume/density—to capture a holistic view of structural alterations. The integration of a spatial attention mechanism (SEBlock) enables the architecture to selectively prioritize biologically relevant regions. The model was rigorously validated across two independent clinical centers (adults from Hangzhou and adolescents from Jinan). Results MAN-MDDNet significantly outperformed traditional machine learning and baseline deep learning models, achieving accuracies of 85.90%–87.18% across the two clinical centers. Notably, t-SNE revealed high structural heterogeneity in the non-remission group, indicating complex resistance mechanisms. Conclusion This study presents an interpretable deep learning framework that integrates multi-feature sMRI to predict antidepressant treatment response, which may assist in personalized management of MDD.

title: Imaging-driven early intervention for BAV-IE with atypical symptoms and severe multisystem complications: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is the most prevalent congenital cardiac malformation and confers a markedly elevated risk of infective endocarditis (IE).Severe concurrent complications, including perivalvular abscess, ruptured aortic sinus aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, and complete atrioventricular block(AVB), rarely coexist in a single patient, and afebrile atypical presentations further delay diagnosis. Cardiac computed tomography angiography (CTA) enables comprehensive preoperative anatomical mapping for complex BAV-IE, yet standardized imaging-driven management experience for this extreme disease spectrum remains scarce. Methods We report a 59-year-old afebrile male patient presenting with 4 months of exertional dyspnea. Preoperative cardiac CTA with 3D volume rendering was performed to delineate valvular, perivalvular, and aortic root lesions.A composite radical Bentall-based surgical procedure was delivered, with postoperative blood culture and 3-year serial echocardiographic follow-up. All imaging data were anonymized for publication. Results CTA confirmed congenital type 0 BAV, IE with perivalvular abscess, 18 mm coronary sinus rupture forming a 5.0×4.5 cm aortic root pseudoaneurysm, and third-degree atrioventricular block.Intraoperative debridement combined with aortic root replacement, multi-valvular repair, and temporary epicardial pacing was completed successfully.Streptococcus mitis was isolated from blood cultures.Over three years of follow-up, the mechanical valve remained functionally stable, graft flow stayed unobstructed, and all clinical symptoms completely resolved. Conclusions Cardiac CTA with 3D visualization provides definitive preoperative anatomical stratification for multi-complicated atypical BAV-IE.Early radical composite surgery guided by comprehensive imaging yields a favorable long-term prognosis, even in elderly afebrile patients with four concurrent severe cardiovascular complications.This case highlights the irreplaceable role of multimodal cardiac imaging in risk stratification and surgical planning for complex BAV-associated endocarditis.

title: Zellweger Syndrome in a Neonate: Early Clinical Presentation and Diagnostic Challenges
abstract: Abstract Background Zellweger spectrum disease includes Zellweger syndrome (ZS), a rare autosomal recessive peroxisomal biogenesis condition brought on by mutations in PEX genes. Neurological problems, craniofacial dysmorphism, hepatic failure, renal cysts, and developmental delay are among the multisystem involvement that characterise it. The condition is seldom linked to gastrointestinal abnormalities such jejunal atresia. Due to overlapping clinical characteristics with other newborn disorders, early identification is still difficult. Case presentation : A male newborn who was two months old showed signs of generalised hypotonia, lethargy, and poor eating. There were no notable prenatal or perinatal problems, and the baby was delivered at term with normal APGAR (Appearance, pulse, grimace, activity and respiration) ratings. The newborn experienced delayed meconium passage, bilious vomiting, feeding intolerance, and abdominal distension at 48 hours of life. The resection of the dilated bowel segment as well as primary jejunojejunostomy were used to treat Type IIIb jejunal atresia (apple-peel deformity), which was verified by exploratory laparotomy. Feeding and bowel function improved during the uncomplicated postoperative recovery. Further testing was necessary due to persistent hypotonia & dysmorphic facial traits, such as hypertelorism, a sunken nasal bridge, a large forehead, and low-set ears. Hepatomegaly and bilateral renal cortical cysts were seen on ultrasonography. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed caudothalamic germinolytic cysts, perisylvian polymicrogyria, and bilateral frontoparietal pachygyria. The diagnosis of Zellweger syndrome was confirmed by genetic investigation that revealed pathogenic mutations in the PEX1 gene and metabolic evaluation that revealed high blood very long-chain fatty acids. Genetic counselling and multidisciplinary supportive care were started. Conclusion This instance emphasises how crucial it is to take underlying genetic and metabolic problems into account when newborns exhibit congenital gastrointestinal abnormalities and multisystem involvement. The condition is seldom linked to gastrointestinal abnormalities such jejunal atresia. Due to overlapping clinical characteristics with other newborn disorders, early identification is still difficult. The resection of the dilated bowel segment as well as primary jejunojejunostomy were used to treat Type IIIb jejunal atresia (apple-peel deformity), which was verified by exploratory laparotomy. Feeding and bowel function improved during the uncomplicated postoperative recovery. Further testing was necessary due to persistent hypotonia & dysmorphic facial traits, such as hypertelorism, a sunken nasal bridge, a large forehead, and low-set ears. Hepatomegaly and bilateral renal cortical cysts were seen on ultrasonography. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed caudothalamic germinolytic cysts, perisylvian polymicrogyria, and bilateral frontoparietal pachygyria. The diagnosis of Zellweger syndrome was confirmed by genetic investigation that revealed pathogenic mutations in the PEX1 gene and metabolic evaluation that revealed high blood very long-chain fatty acids. Genetic counselling and multidisciplinary supportive care were started. Conclusion This instance emphasises how crucial it is to take underlying genetic and metabolic problems into account when newborns exhibit congenital gastrointestinal abnormalities and multisystem involvement. Accurate diagnosis, supportive care, prognosis evaluation, and genetic counselling all depend on early detection and interdisciplinary assessment.

title: Intraoperative technology in skull base and vascular neurosurgery: a two-stage cross-sectional national survey
abstract: Abstract Background: Skull base and vascular neurosurgery rely on diverse intraoperative technologies. Although many are well established, contemporary data describing real-world usage patterns across operative paradigms are limited. We aimed to characterise national practice and variation in intraoperative technology use within these surgical fields. Methods: We conducted a two-stage cross-sectional survey of UK and Ireland neurosurgeons via the Society of British Neurological Surgeons (SBNS). Six SBNS MedTech Committee members compiled a predefined technology list. Respondents then reported frequency of use of these technologies for three exemplar procedures: transsphenoidal approaches for pituitary adenomas, retrosigmoid approaches for vestibular schwannomas, and pterional approaches for intracranial aneurysms. Use was recorded on a four-point ordinal scale and analysed descriptively. Kendall’s tau-b rank correlation explored the relationship between surgeon experience and technology use. Results: Twenty-four responses from 21 British neurosurgical units (66% of adult/mixed units) were analysed. Technology use was strongly procedure specific. Neuronavigation was common for transsphenoidal surgery but less frequent for retrosigmoid and pterional approaches. Endoscopy displaced microscopy in transsphenoidal surgery, whereas microscopy remained dominant for retrosigmoid and pterional approaches. Indocyanine green video angiography and micro-Doppler ultrasonography were widely used for aneurysm vascular visualisation. Drills were common across procedures, alongside micro-debriders (transsphenoidal) and ultrasonic aspirators (retrosigmoid). Neurophysiological monitoring was universal in vestibular schwannoma surgery and variably used for aneurysms. Newer technologies, including augmented reality, exoscopes, intraoperative MRI, and robotics, were used infrequently. Surgeon experience showed no significant association with technology use. Conclusions: Intraoperative technology use in British skull base and vascular neurosurgery is strongly shaped by operative paradigms. Established technologies cluster around recurring procedural needs: orientation, visualisation, tissue manipulation, and neurophysiological monitoring. Newer technologies remain selectively adopted, with uptake likely influenced by cost, infrastructure, training requirements, and workflow compatibility.

title: Upper Airway Morphology on Lateral Radiographs and Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Outcome
abstract: Abstract Purpose Treatment response to hypoglossal nerve stimulation (HNS) for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) remains variable despite stringent selection criteria. We evaluated whether upper airway anatomy and electrode cuff position on postoperative lateral radiographs are associated with HNS treatment response. Methods Postoperative lateral radiographs were analyzed using standardized cephalometric measurements of the spatial relationships between the hyoid bone, mandible, cervical spine, and electrode cuff. The primary outcome was reduction in the apnea–hypopnea index (AHI). Secondary outcomes included associations between radiographic measurements, responder status according to the Sher criteria, and baseline characteristics. Results Fifty-three patients (23% female) with a median age of 62.4 years and median body mass index of 27.0 kg/m² were included. Median AHI decreased from 39.3 (interquartile range, IQR, 25.8–51.8) to 24.3 (IQR, 12.6–35.4) events/hour (P < .001). Among all measurements, only the angle between the hyoid bone and electrode cuff correlated with absolute AHI reduction (Spearman’s rho = 0.39, 95% CI 0.14–0.60; adjusted P = .029). Responders also exhibited a larger angle between the hyoid bone and electrode cuff, although this was not significant after adjustment for multiple testing (P = .042; adjusted P = .111). No other radiographic parameter was associated with treatment response. Conclusion HNS significantly improved objective and subjective outcomes; however, static upper airway anatomy and electrode cuff position on lateral radiographs showed limited value for predicting treatment response. These findings suggest that non-anatomical factors, including upper airway collapsibility and arousal threshold, may contribute more to HNS outcomes than static anatomy.

title: Effects of Preoperative Coenzyme Q10 Supplementation on Oxidative Stress and Wound Healing Following Orthognathic Surgery: A Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial
abstract: Abstract Objective Oxidative stress influences postoperative wound healing after orthognathic surgery. Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10), a mitochondrial antioxidant, may reduce oxidative stress and support tissue repair. This randomized placebo-controlled trial evaluated the effects of preoperative CoQ10 supplementation on postoperative wound healing. Materials and methods Twenty patients undergoing orthognathic surgery were randomly assigned to receive CoQ10 (300 mg/day) or placebo for 2 weeks before surgery. Serum CoQ10 and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels were measured on surgery day and 1 week postoperatively. Wound healing–related markers ( FGF2 , COL1A1 , and TNF-α ) were evaluated by RT-qPCR at 4 weeks postoperatively. Jaw function was assessed by maximum mouth opening immediately after intermaxillary fixation removal and 1 month thereafter. Facial swelling was quantified using three-dimensional facial volumetric analysis immediately after surgery and at 1 and 4 weeks postoperatively. Bone regeneration was evaluated radiographically using CBCT immediately after surgery and at 6 months postoperatively. Results Serum CoQ10 levels were significantly higher in CoQ10 group on surgery day (p = 0.023). The percentage increase in MDA levels was significantly lower compared with the control group (p = 0.038). FGF2 expression was significantly upregulated at 4 weeks (p = 0.028), whereas COL1A1 and TNF-α showed no significant intergroup differences. No significant differences were observed in facial swelling, functional recovery, or relative bone density. Conclusion and Clinical relevance: Preoperative CoQ10 supplementation may modulate oxidative stress and molecular pathways involved in postoperative wound healing after orthognathic surgery. However, these molecular changes did not translate into measurable clinical improvements within the timeframe evaluated. Trial registration: Registered in Thai Clinical Trials Registry (https://www.thaiclinicaltrials.org/export/pdf/TCTR20260201003) under the registration number TCTR20260201003; retrospectively registered on 1 February 2026.
